newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters resigned or cynical; no outrage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters resigned or cynical; no outrage.

text.p: Bob Dole's angry question -- "Where is the outrage in America?" -- has found some uneasy answers from U.S. political experts who find indifference, cynicism and resignation dominant among U.S. voters.

Dole posed the question on the campaign trail after trying and failing to set the electorate afire with charges about President Bill Clinton's character, campaign fund-raising and policies. Nothing worked.
Finally Dole, the Republican presidential candidate, exploded at a rally in Houston last week: "Where is the outrage in America? Where is the outrage in America? Where has the media gone in America?"

His words echoed in Washington with less than a week to go before the Nov. 5 election in a presidential campaign that has generated little excitement since Dole prevailed as his party's choice for the White House last spring. Dole has never led Clinton in any national poll and currently trails the Democratic incumbent by double digits.

"There is a lot to be outraged about," said Ann McBride, whose Common Cause citizens' lobby has reported massive violations of campaign finance laws by both the Dole and Clinton camps. "It's out of control," McBride said on Wednesday on ABC's Good Morning America programme.

Pollster John Zogby believes voters feel a sense of resignation about their own lives and the country's politics, as indicated by one arresting statistic: a large slice of Americans answer "no" when asked if their current job pays less than their last job.

At first this sounds like good economic news, but on further examination Zogby found that many of these respondents were on their second low-paying job, having already weathered a drop in income years before.

"We're moving into a period of adjusted expectations," he said by telephone. "It's one thing if you're clobbered over the head with a hammer once ... When you're clobbered the second time the odds are there's going to be some permanent damage."

And the vast majority of voters who favoured Clinton or were undecided in the weeks before the election told pollsters their vote would not change even if they knew beforehand that Clinton's re-election would lead to charges that this second term was the most corrupt of the century, Zogby said.

Stephen Hess, who has worked for both Democratic and Republican presidents dating back to Dwight Eisenhower, said voters are not resigned, they are indifferent to politics, despite flurries of interest in the 1992 and 1994 elections.

"Americans have to be agitated, irritated or energised by something ... either that something is going wrong with the economy or that something is going wrong with the world and Americans are being placed in harm's way," said Hess, who now works for the Brookings Institution think tank. "When this isn't around, there just isn't much outrage in the system."

Michigan Gov. John Engler, who has campaigned with Dole and heads the Republican Governors Association, blamed the growing cynical mood that may have begun with the Watergate scandal that brought down President Richard Nixon in 1974.

"I think unfortunately over the last 22 years there has been a commensurate rise in electoral cynicism," Engler said in a telephone news conference. He also said the Clinton Administration had been able to shrug off reported scandals as "mere politics," leaving voters no way to judge how serious the reported offences may be.

For Terry Jeffries, a conservative journalist who used to manage Pat Buchanan's presidential campaign, the fault lies not with the candidates but with the media. "The liberal media in this election has basically suspended hard and tough reporting," Jeffries said.
But he said the so-called Republican revolutionaries who took control of Congress in 1994 could wake voters up. "The cynicism's going to go away."
